FROMLIST: PM / mfd: intel-lpss: Push system sleep callbacks to late/early stages Push the system suspend/resume callbacks of intel-lpss to the late suspend/early resume stages to allow child device callbacks to be pushed to the late/early stages of suspend/resume too, so as to make it possible to avoid resuming the children if they are runtime- suspended during system suspend going forward. Signed-off-by: Rafael J. Wysocki <rafael.j.wysocki@intel.com> (am from ttps://patchwork.kernel.org/patch/9939809/) BUG=b:63121330 TEST=verify that no failures from camera suspend/resume time. Change-Id: I748b2398cb8d4ff717f9ab49496de0b015638a00 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/676272 Commit-Ready: Rajat Jain <rajatja@chromium.org> Tested-by: Rajat Jain <rajatja@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Furquan Shaikh <furquan@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Hyungwoo Yang <hyungwoo.yang@intel.com>

FROMLIST/BACKPORT: PM / i2c: designware: Clean up system sleep handling After commit a23318feeff6 (i2c: designware: Fix system suspend) the i2c-designware-platdrv driver always resumes the device in its system sleep ->suspend callback which isn't particularly nice, even though it is technically correct. A better approach would be to make the driver track the PM state of the device so that it doesn't need to resume it in ->suspend, so implement it. First, drop dw_i2c_plat_suspend() added by commit a23318feeff6 and rename dw_i2c_plat_runtime_suspend() back to dw_i2c_plat_suspend(). Second, point the driver's ->late_suspend and ->early_resume callbacks, rather than its ->suspend and ->resume callbacks, to dw_i2c_plat_suspend() and dw_i2c_plat_resume(), respectively, so that they are not executed in parallel with each other, for example if runtime resume of the device takes place during system suspend. Finally, add "suspended" and "skip_resume" flags to struct dw_i2c_dev and make dw_i2c_plat_suspend() and dw_i2c_plat_resume() use them to avoid suspending or resuming the device twice in a row and to avoid resuming a previously runtime-suspended device during system resume. Overrides: a23318feeff6 (i2c: designware: Fix system suspend) Signed-off-by: Rafael J. Wysocki <rafael.j.wysocki@intel.com> (backported from https://patchwork.kernel.org/patch/9939807/) BUG=b:63121330 TEST=verify that no failures from camera suspend/resume time. CHROMIUM: iwl7000: pcie: dump registers when HW becomes inaccessible We conclude the HW became inaccessible when we timeout waiting for a bit to be set in a memory mapped register (CSR_GP_CNTRL). This conclusion may not be true because the bit may not get set due to: - a firmware issue - a driver issue - a PCI bus issue - a platform issue There are a lot of such reports with really no good debug information beyond this message to help us. Add some debug information and attempt to dump the different register spaces at such a failure: * Dump some configuration space of device - this will tell us if something very basic is broken in the PCIe bus (so that configuration accesses are failing). If this works, the PCIe bus seems OK. If this does not work, it is definitely an PCIe issue. * Dump some memory mapped registers - if we're reading some sane'ish values, this will tell us that the PCIe bus is OK, but may be a firmware / driver issue. If this does not work, it may be a PCI configuration issue or a driver/firmware issue. * Dump parent and device's AER registers, will give us some straws to chew on. Fizz: Limit input current Fizz has an over current control system. There are two FETs connected to two registers: PR257 & PR258. They control the max input current as follows: PR257, PR258 For 4.62A (90W BJ adapter), on, off For 3.33A (65W BJ adapter), off, on For 3.00A (Type-C adapter), off, off BJ adapters are distinguished by reading GPIO71. This patch also removes ISL9238 driver and ramping code. The charger chip has been removed from the board since proto2. BUG=b:65013352 BRANCH=none TEST=Boot Fizz Proto3 on BJ and Type-C. Change-Id: I32c2467f4ab23adf3f9313a03914d74d64a722df Signed-off-by: Daisuke Nojiri <dnojiri@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/668119 Reviewed-by: Aaron Durbin <adurbin@chromium.org>

[autotest] Add job_aborter Add the skeleton of job_aborter. All of the cases that job_aborter has to handle are added. Due to considerations for job_aborter that came up, existing code has been redesigned. 1. The implementation for aborting a job has been moved out. The existing design is unnecessarily complex. The abort signaling mechanism should not need to go through job_reporter and can be handled directly by job_shepherd. Since job_shepherd is written in Go, the async aspect of that will be much easier to write than the Python async that would be needed for job_reporter to play middleman. The new logic will be added to monitor_db, job_aborter, and job_shepherd; job_reporter need not play. 2. Job lease liveness is determined by fcntl locks. This is more reliable than working with pids and/or sending signals. (As a bonus, this prevents a job from being owned by two processes at the same in certain cases.) bluetooth: "Fix" sync of commands for adv & scan This is a very ugly hack, presented here in a very ugly way. The ugly way is basically how we deliver this only for eve and not affect other devices. The ugly hack is basically how we work aroung bluez's complete lack of synchronization. Let me explain. No, there is not time. Let me summarize: bluez has a boolean value for "are we scanning" which it updates inside the command-complete event handler. It also checks this in many places as a way to tell if the chip is or is not scanning. The issue is that some chips (like BCM's) let you disable something already disabled and do not raise a fuss. Other chips (like Intel's 7265) do raise a fuss if you try to disable scanning if it is already off. So why the issue? If the chip raises an error, bluez loses its marbles and gets out of sync with the chip. Basically it thinks the chip *IS* scanning while chip is not. There is no way out of this since any attempt to tell bluez to start scanning causes it to just reply with "already am" and any attempt to stop scanning sends the "scan disable" command to the chip and produces the same kind of error that got us into this mess. So how do we fix this? There isn't really a simple or elegant way. But the basic issue is that while a command to enable or disable scanning is in flight, any code in the stack will think scanning is still in the old state, while it may already be in the new state. This might cause more commands to be enqueued based on this errorneous information. To solve this we'd like to always have correct information. Sadly this is not easy. There is also a command queue, which at any point in time may have many command enqueued that affect scanning state. There are multiple ways to insert commands into it, and we do not want to instrument them all. So what do we do? First we add a second boolean bit for "scan state change command in flight". We set this when we *SEND TO THE CHIP* a command that affects scan state and clear it when a reply arrives. We also change all places that check the "are we scanning" state to properly consider this new variable as well. This will not solve the issue of many commands queued already. So it is still possible that while a "disable" was queued, another "disable" may be queued. To work around this we also track the current state in the lowest layer that actually sends commands to the chip and simply drop ones that would transition us to the same state that we're already in. The situation is actually weirder because there is a "restart" func in bluez all of whose callers seem to assume that it atomically toggles scanning off and back on if it is already on. No such atomicity exists in reality. Our hack covers up for this in most cases. Oh, and this same exact logic applies to "are we advertising" boolean and we treat it the same way. This really solves nothing, but it works around the issue well enough for our purposes. A proper fix would be a separate queue for state changes for "adv" and "scan" with proper suport for atomic "restart" requests. This queue would then submit actual commands to the chip's queue. since nobody else would do that, it would have no races. We have no time to produce such fixes, so for now you get to enjoy this dirty hack. This hack is based on initial work by josephsih@ who first figured out the proper place to filter all the low level commands as they are sent to the chip and the proper way to drop them.
